text: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and get min, which retrieves the minimum element. All four operations must run in constant time.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — get min returns the smallest value currently in the stack, and it must be constant time, so I can't scan the stack on each call. Right?
Correct. All four operations are constant time.
One thing to pin down. After I pop the current minimum, get min must return the previous minimum. So the structure has to remember minimums as they change, not just the latest one.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would be to scan the whole stack on every get min. That's linear time per call, too slow. A single min variable is also broken: once I pop that minimum, I've lost the runner-up. This problem reminds me of a running prefix minimum, stored right on the stack. Each cell keeps a pair: the value, and the minimum so far. Then get min just reads the top's second field, and the minimum rides along with its element through push and pop.

Here's the plan. One: each cell holds the value and the minimum of this cell and everything below it. Two: on push, if the stack is empty store the value twice, otherwise store the value with the smaller of the value and the top's min. Three: top reads the value, get min reads the min, and pop just pops. One thing worth flagging — the invariant. Each cell's stored min is the minimum of itself and everything below it. So the top's min is the whole stack's min. And after a pop, the new top already holds the right answer, with no recompute. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The stack holds pairs of value and min so far. Push is the only method with logic: on an empty stack the value is its own min; otherwise I read the old top's min through get min, take the smaller of that and the value, and push the pair. Pop, top and get min each touch only the top. One thing worth flagging — the empty-stack guard in push is essential. Without it, the very first push would call get min, which reads top on an empty stack. That's undefined behavior.

Let's dry-run it. Push five, two, seven, one, then get min, pop, get min. After the four pushes, get min returns one. The row that matters is the pop. Popping the pair one, one exposes seven, two, whose stored min is two — set back when seven was pushed, because seven is bigger, so it carried the old min forward. So get min instantly returns two, with no recompute. Let's also test corner cases. Push, pop to empty, and push again works: the guard rebuilds the first cell. Repeated minimums like two, two also work, since each cell carries its own min.

The time complexity is constant for all four operations, since each one only touches the top. The space complexity is linear: one extra int per element. Oh, one more thing — I could save space with a second min stack that only pushes when a value is less than or equal to the current min, and pops when the popped value equals its top. Same idea, tighter memory.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You saw immediately that a single min variable breaks on pop. You framed the invariant precisely: each cell's min covers itself and everything below. And you flagged the empty-stack guard as a correctness requirement. Good work.
